4315.tone: Two-level tone reported by three lines: Bromley 1973: 15: 'Only the language spoken at Naltja has been studied in any detail; it is clearly tonal, with two contrastive levels demonstrated (Bromley ms).' Though I have not found any minimal pair in Nalca and Kosarek, the development of (non) phonemic tones can be explained by two processes: (1) Two syllables are contracted into one... cp. Bime ambotum, Eipo ambosum [ambo'tʰóm], Nalca ampum [am'pʰóm] 'yesterday'.... (2) High rising tone is conditioned by the presence or loss of word final glottal stop.' On stress itself: only Wälchli's phrase 'distinctive stress' (credited to the unreachable 1972 ms) and Heeschen's single transcribed form with stress on the contracted final syllable; no source states where stress falls.

4320.heavy: Not spelled out in Geraghty's own words for NNS. The rule is named 'measure-penultimate stress (Schutz 1976)'; in Schütz's analysis a measure (accent unit) is a long syllable (long vowel or diphthong) or two short syllables (Schütz 1985 pp. 107-108, consists of at least one MEASURE (i.e. accent unit)'). Geraghty's own text gives (a) the unqualified rule counts vowels (Lau raíca = penultimate vowel of raica), (b) a rising sequence ai/au is stressed on its first vowel, so it behaves as one heavy unit (ráica, ráuta), and (c) long vowels 'are disallowed before an unstressed syllable by a phonotactic constraint common to all Fijian languages' (pp. 153-154), i.e. long vowels are stressed.
4320.prule: Penultimate stress, stated as 'the penultimate stress rule' (p. 68) and identified as 'the general principle of measure-penultimate stress (Schutz 1976)' (pp. 160-161). The rule counts vowels/moras, not syllables: unqualified, it gives Lau raíca (penultimate vowel i of raica), which Geraghty says 'simply conforms to measure-penultimate stress'; everywhere else, including NNS, it is qualified so that a rising vowel sequence (low or mid vowel + high vowel: ai, au) is stressed on its first vowel (ráica 'see it', ráuta 'enough'). Long vowels are disallowed before an unstressed syllable (pp. 153-154), i.e. a long vowel is always stressed. Stated for all communalects surveyed except Lau (LAU, VBL), so it covers Batiwai, Tubai and Yemalu.

4322.prule: Primary stress on the initial syllable of the phonological word in every word type Reid treats: monomorphemic nominals, free particles and postpositions (p. 90); reduplications and compounds (initial syllable of the first morpheme, pp. 91-92); class-prefixed nouns (the prefix, as the initial syllable of the phonological word, carries the primary stress; class proclitics stand outside the word, pp. 93-95); simple verbs (initial syllable = bound subject pronoun, pp. 95-96); complex verbs (initial syllable of the auxiliary, p. 97). Weight plays no role; final syllables of nominals never bear stress.
4322.srule: Monomorphemic nominals, free particles/postpositions and simple verbs: secondary stress on every second syllable after the initial primary (3rd, 5th...), never on the word-final syllable. Compounds: secondary stress on the initial syllable of each non-initial morpheme regardless of syllable count (contiguous stresses occur). Simple verbs with an object-pronoun suffix: secondary on the suffix-initial syllable. Complex verbs: secondary stress on the initial syllable of the complex verb stem (copied onto both halves of a reduplicated root) and on the initial syllable of a serialised auxiliary; tense/aspect enclitics never stressed.

4324.heavy: Four-step scale by syllable structure alone: CVVN > CVV > CVN > CV (p. 59; only nasal codas occur). Integrated word-level scale Quant > QualPW > Coda > QualFT (p. 66): quantity (long vowel or long diphthong) outranks vowel quality (a > e,o > i; short diphthong æi > i), which in turn outranks coda presence for word stress. CV and CVN are monomoraic, CVV bimoraic.
4324.dflt: All-light words: vowel height decides (a > e,o > i), e.g. (pi.ká)(bi.rì).ti] 'you get going' p. 58; with equal quality, iambic L-to-R feet, no PrWd-final foot, rightmost eligible foot head: CV.CV initial (5a,b p. 50), (i.rì)(pi.rí).ni.te] 'he will sit' (σ4 of 6) and (sá.bi).ta.ka] (σ1 of 4, No-Final-Foot > Rightmost) p. 63.
4324.prule: Prominence-driven (unbounded) weight-sensitive system: word-level (primary) stress goes to the strongest syllable of the prosodic word on the scale Quant > QualPW > Coda (CVVN > CVV > CVN > CV; within a quantity class vowel height a > e,o > i and diphthong > monophthong; closed > open only at equal vowel strength); among ties the rightmost is stressed; a light ultima (CV, CVN) is never stressed; a heavy (CVV, CVVN) ultima is stressed when it is the strongest syllable.
4324.srule: Foot-level (secondary) stress (C&M 2005, verb data): the prosodic word (excluding extraprosodic object/modal clitics) is parsed left-to-right into bisyllabic feet, non-exhaustively: no degenerate feet and no PrWd-final foot unless one is needed to put word stress on the strongest syllable, so a light ultima and, in even-parity words, the penult normally stay unstressed. Each non-primary foot is headed by its stronger syllable on the foot-level Strength scale Quant > Coda > QualFT (CVVN > CVV > CVN > CV; a > e,o > i; æi > i); when the two syllables tie, headship follows Rhythm: iambic by default ('stress is assigned to the second syllable from the left edge and alternatingly thereafter, excluding the ultima', p. 51), trochaic only to avoid a clash with a following stressed syllable (*Clash > Iambic > Trochaic). Michael 2008 (§6.2.3.1, pp. 232, 234) reports the same left-to-right disyllabic iambic

4326.tone: Two level tones, H and L; the tone-bearing unit is the mora, and post-vocalic glides and sonorant consonants also carry tone; each mora of a long vowel is toned independently; falling and rising contours on bimoraic (CVV, CVC) syllables and rising-falling on trimoraic ones are analysed as H/L sequences (falling-rising is ruled out by the phrase constraint); on CVC syllables closed by an obstruent the obstruent mora's tone is realised as a contour on the preceding short vowel; within a phonological phrase an expected H on the syntactic head is dropped whenever combining the words' lexical patterns would create two non-contiguous H tones (pp. 249-250, citing Hayward 2000). On stress the source says only that Thompson's (1976: 484) 'tentative comments about stress' find 'no convincing evidence' and that his examples are better analysed as gemination of the following consonant. Thompson 1976 p. 484 itself gives §2.2 'Stress may come on any syllable and can cause change of meaning' with the 'CVCV -> 'CVCCV gemination rule, and §2.3 'At least two significant tones occur; normal and high' (desso/déssó, du/dú). Reinisch 1874 (pp. 19-20, 61; Munzinger's acute) describes an 'accent' confined to one of the last three syllables that most plausibly records the H tone; no tone is recognised there.

4327.prule: Word tone, not stress. 4327.tone: The source calls the system 'word tone' and never uses 'stress' for Narak (a full-text search of the front matter hits only 'acute accent' = the diacritic). Pronunciation guide (p. 22): 'á, é, í, ó, ú say these vowels on a higher or stronger pitch than the other vowels in the word.' Four patterns contrast in shape on the same final syllable (high-level vs upglide vs high-falling), so this is not accent placement alone; the tone peak is nonetheless positionally restricted to the final or penultimate syllable, and the choice among patterns is partly conditioned by the final segment (obstruent-final and i/u+nasal-final words high-level; a/e/o+liquid-final words upglide; open-final descending words penult-high; liquid-closed descending words final-falling). OPD p. 3, under the template heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': 'Narak has four distinct contrasting tones: high-falling, falling, level and rising tones. Only the last two syllables of the word carry the contrastive tone pattern.' - the heading is answered with tone only, nothing on stress or length.

'Accent'/'syllabe accentuée' is never defined phonetically or phonologically; it appears only as a positional label (stem-initial = accented; proclitic pronoun = pre-accentual; suffixes = post-accentual) conditioning allophony: /p t c k/ voiceless in initial/accented syllables and voiced intervocalically in unaccented syllables (§2.2.1, §4.8.2); short unrounded vowels optionally centralized 'dans le voisinage d'une syllabe accentuée' (§4.9, rules 1-2). tn.quote: Le système tonal ndambomo repose sur l’opposition entre deux tons ponctuels: le ton haut (mwánɛ̀ « enfant ») et le ton bas (ŋwànɛ̀ « bouche »). Les paires minimales suivantes illustrent cette opposition tonale de base: nʧì « mouche (var.) » vs ǹʧí « cou » ... Le ton moyen, qui y est également attesté, pourrait être la réalisation d’un ton haut devant pause ... Nous avons considéré ces tons descendants comme des réalisations particulières du haut devant pause ... Sur les substantifs, nous avons recensé les schèmes tonals B, H, BH et HB.
tn.translation: The Ndambomo tone system rests on the opposition between two level (punctual) tones: the high tone (mwánɛ̀ 'child') and the low tone (ŋwànɛ̀ 'mouth'). The following minimal pairs illustrate this basic tonal opposition: nʧì 'fly (var.)' vs ǹʧí 'neck' ... The mid tone, which is also attested, could be the realisation of a high tone before pause ... We have treated these falling tones as particular realisations of high before pause ... On nouns we have recorded the tone schemes L, H, LH and HL.

tn.note: Two level tones H, L; mid, falling, rising are realisations (H before pause; L+H); downstepped H in some HH verbs, floating L called probable; noun schemes L H LH HL, verbs LH HL; nothing on stress.

tn.quote: Ndonga, like all the other southern Bantu languages is a tone language, which is to say that the pitches on an utterance play a significant part in contrasts between lexical forms as well as in grammatical signalling. It is impossible to conceive of a comprehensive reference grammar of this language in which tone is not treated. ... the interpretation of the clearly audible pitches of the language in terms of a system is a complex matter. ... the tonal system in particular calls for more careful investigation than was possible in the time available for this study.
